title: Choosing the right syringe or measure for the volume
blurb: Pick the smallest syringe or measure that holds the whole dose and is marked finely enough to measure it exactly.
question: A child needs 0.24 mL of an oral medicine. Oral syringes of 1 mL (marked every 0.01 mL), 3 mL (every 0.1 mL) and 5 mL (every 0.2 mL) are available. Which should be used?

teach.h: Two tests for the right device
teach.body: The right syringe or measure passes two tests. It must hold the whole volume in one go, and its smallest marks must land exactly on the volume. Plain English: choose the smallest device that holds the dose and has a mark on it at that exact volume. A large syringe has wide marks, so small volumes cannot be measured accurately in it.

head: Volume
Usual choice
Why
rows: pot only for multiples of its marks
teach.caption: Oral liquids are measured with oral syringes (or a pot), not with syringes intended for injection.

teach.body: Divide the volume by the mark value. A whole number means the volume falls exactly on a mark. 3.4 ÷ 0.2 = 17: measurable on a 5 mL syringe marked every 0.2 mL. 3.5 ÷ 0.2 = 17.5: not measurable, so choose a syringe marked every 0.1 mL.

items: Staff nurse Daniel Evans needs 2.4 mL of paracetamol suspension for a child.
Medicine pot marked every 2.5 mL: 2.4 ÷ 2.5 is not a whole number, so it fails.
1 mL syringe: too small to hold 2.4 mL in one draw.
5 mL oral syringe marked every 0.2 mL: holds it, and 2.4 ÷ 0.2 = 12, a whole number.
He uses the 5 mL oral syringe and draws up to the second small mark above 2.

teach.text: Using a big syringe for a tiny volume (0.35 mL in a 10 mL syringe marked every 0.5 mL) cannot give an accurate dose, and repeated fills of a tiny syringe multiply the measuring error. Choose the smallest device that holds the whole volume and has an exact mark.

items: The device must hold the whole volume in one go.
Volume ÷ mark value must be a whole number.
Pick the smallest device that passes both tests.
Pots suit larger volumes in multiples of 2.5 or 5 mL.
Measure oral liquids with an oral syringe or pot.

summary: You can now work out the value of each mark on a device, test whether a volume falls exactly on a mark, and choose the smallest syringe or measure that holds the whole dose accurately.

A.q: A volume of 3.6 mL is to be measured in one draw. Syringes of 1 mL, 2 mL, 5 mL and 10 mL are available, each marked every 0.1 mL or finer. What is the capacity of the smallest syringe that holds the whole volume? Please use the correct unit.
A.why: The smallest capacity of at least 3.6 mL is 5 mL.

whyNot.0: A 2 mL syringe cannot hold 3.6 mL in one draw.
whyNot.2: This holds the volume but is not the smallest that does.
whyNot.3: A 1 mL syringe would need four draws.

A.q: A 10 mL syringe has 50 equal small spaces between 0 and 10 mL. What volume does each small space represent? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.1: Divided 50 by 10; divide the volume by the spaces.

A.q: A volume of 0.45 mL is to be measured in a 1 mL syringe marked every 0.01 mL. How many small marks above zero should the front edge of the seal reach?

whyNot.0: Divided 0.45 by 0.1; the marks are 0.01 mL.
whyNot.1: Divided 0.45 by 0.05; the marks are 0.01 mL.
whyNot.2: Divided 0.45 by 0.001; the marks are 0.01 mL.

B.q: A child needs 0.24 mL of an oral medicine. Oral syringes of 1 mL (marked every 0.01 mL), 3 mL (every 0.1 mL), 5 mL (every 0.2 mL) and 10 mL (every 0.5 mL) are available. Which capacity measures the dose exactly? Please use the correct unit.
B.why: Only the 1 mL syringe (0.01 mL marks) has a mark at 0.24 mL: 0.24 ÷ 0.01 = 24.

whyNot.0: 0.24 mL does not fall on a 0.1 mL mark.
whyNot.2: 0.24 mL does not fall on a 0.2 mL mark.
whyNot.3: 0.24 mL does not fall on a 0.5 mL mark.

B.q: A dose of 35 mL is to be given using a 10 mL oral syringe. What is the least number of times the syringe must be filled?
B.why: 35 ÷ 10 = 3.5, so 4 fills (three full and one of 5 mL).

whyNot.0: Three fills give 30 mL, which is 5 mL short.
whyNot.1: You cannot fill a syringe half a time; count whole fills.
whyNot.2: Five fills could give 50 mL; four are enough.

B.q: A volume of 1.3 mL is needed. Syringes available: 1 mL (marked every 0.01 mL), 2 mL (every 0.1 mL), 5 mL (every 0.2 mL) and 10 mL (every 0.5 mL). What is the capacity of the smallest syringe that holds and measures 1.3 mL exactly? Please use the correct unit.

whyNot.1: A 1 mL syringe cannot hold 1.3 mL in one draw.
whyNot.2: 1.3 mL does not fall on a 0.2 mL mark.
whyNot.3: 1.3 mL does not fall on a 0.5 mL mark.

C.q: A child needs 6.6 mL, measured in two draws with a 5 mL oral syringe marked every 0.2 mL. The first draw is a full 5 mL. What volume is the second draw? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
C.why: 6.6 - 5 = 1.6 mL; 1.6 ÷ 0.2 = 8 marks, so it can be measured exactly.

whyNot.0: Split the dose into two equal halves; the first draw was 5 mL.
whyNot.1: Added 5 mL to the dose instead of subtracting it.
whyNot.3: Took away 6 mL instead of 5 mL.

C.q: A child is prescribed 4.8 mL and a 5 mL oral syringe marked every 0.2 mL is used. How many small marks above zero should the front edge of the seal reach?

whyNot.0: Counted 0.1 mL per mark; they are 0.2 mL.
whyNot.1: Counted 0.5 mL per mark; they are 0.2 mL.
whyNot.3: Rounded the dose to the nearest whole mL.

C.q: A child is prescribed 84 mg of an oral suspension labelled 120 mg in 5 mL. Oral syringes of 1 mL, 2.5 mL, 5 mL and 10 mL are available, each marked every 0.1 mL. What is the capacity of the smallest syringe that holds the dose in one draw? Please use the correct unit.
C.why: Volume = 84 ÷ 120 x 5 = 3.5 mL. The smallest syringe of at least 3.5 mL is 5 mL.

whyNot.1: The dose is 3.5 mL, more than 2.5 mL.
whyNot.2: This holds it but is not the smallest that does.
whyNot.3: The dose is 3.5 mL, far more than 1 mL.

reteach.title: The snuggest fit
reteach.question: Why not just use a 10 mL syringe for everything?

blocks.body: A 10 mL syringe may only be marked every 0.5 mL, so 0.3 mL sits between marks and has to be guessed. A 1 mL syringe marked every 0.01 mL lands on 0.3 mL exactly. Choose the snuggest fit: the smallest device that still holds the whole dose.

blocks.text: A pot marked every 2.5 mL cannot measure 3 mL or 13 mL; use an oral syringe.

explain.body: Capacity must be at least the volume needed.

test.q: A volume of 8 mL is to be drawn up in one draw. Syringes of 5 mL, 10 mL, 20 mL and 50 mL are available, each with suitable marks. What is the capacity of the smallest suitable syringe? Please use the correct unit.
test.why: The smallest capacity of at least 8 mL is 10 mL.

whyNot.0: A 5 mL syringe cannot hold 8 mL in one draw.
whyNot.1: This holds it but is not the smallest that does.
whyNot.2: This holds it but has wide marks and is far too large.

explain.body: Volume between numbers ÷ number of spaces.

test.q: A 3 mL syringe has 10 equal small spaces in each 1 mL. What volume does each space represent? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.0: Divided the full 3 mL by 10; there are 10 spaces in each 1 mL.
whyNot.2: This is the gap between numbers, not one space.
whyNot.3: Assumed 100 spaces per mL; there are 10.

explain.body: Volume ÷ mark value must give a whole number.

test.q: Which volume can be measured exactly on a 5 mL syringe marked every 0.2 mL?
test.why: 3.4 ÷ 0.2 = 17, a whole number, so 3.4 mL lies on a mark.

explain.body: A pot marked every 2.5 mL measures 2.5, 5, 7.5 mL and so on. Anything in between needs an oral syringe.

test.q: A 30 mL pot is marked every 2.5 mL. Which volume cannot be measured exactly in it?
test.why: 13 ÷ 2.5 = 5.2, so 13 mL falls between marks and needs an oral syringe.
